course: Fortified Corn-Soy Porridge for Malnourished Children
module_title: Scaling Up Production and Managing Workers

lessons.title: Hiring and training local women to help with production
lessons.body: When your porridge business grows beyond what you can handle alone, hire local women. They know the community, are trusted, and often need income. Start by hiring 2â3 women part-time. Pay fairly: in most African countries, a daily wage of 5,000â10,000 shillings (or equivalent) is reasonable for 6 hours of work. Look for women who are reliable, clean, and good with numbers. Ask them to bring a national ID and two references. Train them on the job for one week. Show them how to weigh ingredients, mix properly, and seal bags. Use a simple checklist: 1) Wash hands and wear clean aprons. 2) Measure corn and soy flour exactly (e.g., 70% corn, 30% soy). 3) Add micronutrient premix as instructed. 4) Mix for 10 minutes until uniform color. 5) Seal bags immediately. Let them practice while you watch, then correct mistakes gently. Pay a bonus for bags that pass quality checks. Schedule shifts: morning shift 7amâ1pm, afternoon shift 1pmâ6pm. Provide a free bag of porridge each week as a benefit. Keep records: name, days worked, amount paid. Treat them with respectâthey are your partners. When demand increases, promote the best worker to supervisor with a higher wage. This builds loyalty and reduces turnover.

lessons.title: Setting up a simple production line for efficiency
lessons.body: A production line moves ingredients through steps in order, so you donât waste time walking back and forth. Set up five stations in a straight line or U-shape: 1) Weighing station: digital scale (capacity 5â10 kg), scoops, and containers for corn flour, soy flour, sugar, and premix. 2) Mixing station: a large basin or drum, wooden paddle or hand mixer. 3) Milling station (if you grind your own): a hammer mill or grinder. 4) Packaging station: sealer, measuring cups, bags, and labels. 5) Storage station: sealed buckets or shelves. Keep ingredients on the left, finished bags on the right. Each worker stays at one station and passes the product forward. For example, Worker A weighs 7 kg corn and 3 kg soy into a bucket, passes to Worker B who mixes for 10 minutes, passes to Worker C who scoops 500g into bags and seals. This reduces movement and errors. Use a timer to keep pace: aim for 50 bags per hour with 3 workers. Label each bag with production date and batch number. Clean all stations at the end of the day with soap and water. A simple line like this can triple your output without expensive machinery.

lessons.title: Buying or renting larger equipment: grinders, mixers, sealers
lessons.body: When hand grinding and mixing slows you down, invest in equipment. A diesel-powered hammer mill (e.g., 10â20 HP) costs $800â$2,500 new, or you can rent one for $20â$50 per day from a local agro-dealer. It grinds 100â200 kg per hour. A horizontal mixer (500 kg capacity) costs $1,500â$3,000; a smaller 50 kg mixer costs $300â$600. For sealing, a continuous band sealer costs $150â$400 and seals 20â30 bags per minute. A simple impulse sealer is $30â$80 but slower. If you cannot afford to buy, rent: many towns have equipment rental shops. Or form a cooperative with other porridge makers to share costs. Before buying, calculate: if you produce 500 kg per week, a $1,000 grinder pays for itself in 3â6 months by saving labour and increasing output. Check power source: diesel is common in rural areas; electric needs stable current. Always have spare parts (belts, blades, heating elements) and a trained mechanic. Train one worker to operate and maintain each machine. Safety: wear goggles and gloves, never put hands near moving parts. Clean equipment after every use to prevent rust and contamination. Start with one machine at a timeâgrinder first, then sealer, then mixer.

lessons.title: Quality control checks at each step of production
lessons.body: Quality control means checking every step so the final porridge is safe and nutritious. Step 1: Receiving ingredients. Check corn and soy for mould, insects, or moisture. Moisture should be below 12%âbite a grain, it should crack, not squash. Reject any mouldy bags. Step 2: Weighing. Use a digital scale. Weigh corn, soy, sugar, and premix exactly. For a 10 kg batch: 7 kg corn, 2.8 kg soy, 0.2 kg premix. Record weights in a notebook. Step 3: Mixing. Mix for at least 10 minutes until colour is uniform. Take a handful from three different spotsâif colours differ, mix more. Step 4: Milling. Check grind size: flour should pass through a 1 mm sieve. Too coarse and it wonât cook well. Step 5: Packaging. Seal bags immediately. Check seal by squeezingâno leaks. Weigh 5 random bags per batch; each should be 500g Â± 10g. Step 6: Storage. Keep bags in a cool, dry place off the floor. Use within 3 months. Step 7: Final check. Once a week, cook a small sample and taste. It should smell fresh, not rancid. Keep a QC log: date, batch number, checks done, signature. If a batch fails, do not sell itârework or discard. This protects your reputation and saves lives.

lessons.title: Managing inventory of ingredients and packaging
lessons.body: Inventory management ensures you never run out of ingredients or packaging, and never overstock. Use a simple notebook or a phone app like Excel or Google Sheets. List every item: corn flour, soy flour, sugar, micronutrient premix, bags, labels, and sealer tape. For each, record: quantity in stock, reorder level, and supplier contact. Reorder level = (average daily use Ã lead time) + safety stock. For example, if you use 20 kg corn per day and it takes 3 days to deliver, reorder when stock hits 80 kg (20Ã3 + 20 safety). Count stock every Friday. Write the date and quantity. Keep ingredients in airtight containers on shelves, away from sunlight and moisture. Use FIFO: first in, first out. Put older bags in front. For packaging, buy in bulk to save moneyâe.g., 1,000 bags at once. Store in a dry cupboard. Keep a minimum of 2 weeksâ worth of all items. If you see a shortage coming (e.g., harvest season price rise), buy extra. But donât overbuy perishables like premixâcheck expiry dates. Train one worker as inventory clerk. They update the book daily. You review weekly. A simple inventory system prevents costly delays and keeps production smooth.

lessons.title: Planning for increased demand during emergencies
lessons.body: Emergenciesâfloods, droughts, disease outbreaksâcause sudden spikes in demand for fortified porridge. You must plan ahead. First, keep a buffer stock: 2â4 weeks of ingredients and packaging in a dry, secure room. Second, create an emergency production plan. Identify how you can double output: add a second shift (e.g., 6pmâ10pm), hire 2â3 temporary workers from a pre-trained list, and rent extra equipment. Third, simplify packaging: use plain bags with a sticker instead of printed labels to save time. Fourth, coordinate with local health centres, NGOs, and churches. They can give you advance notice of emergencies and help distribute. Fifth, set a fair price for emergenciesâdonât profiteer. For example, during a cholera outbreak, you might sell at cost to clinics. Sixth, stock extra fuel for diesel grinders. Seventh, practice a mock emergency: once a month, run a drill to produce 200 bags in 4 hours. Time each step. Fix bottlenecks. Eighth, keep cash reserve for emergency wages and transport. Ninth, communicate with your workers: agree they will work extra hours when needed. Pay overtime. Tenth, after the emergency, thank your team and restock. This preparation saves lives and builds your reputation as a reliable supplier.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaling Up Production and Managing Workers

This practical reference is for small and growing African producers of fortified corn-soy porridge who already make consistent batches for their community and now need to serve clinics, schools, NGOs, and emergency markets without losing quality or burning out their team. Scaling up is not simply buying a bigger grinder. It is a system: people, process, equipment, checks, stock, and contingency. The lessons below cover hiring and training local women, building a simple production line, equipment decisions, quality control, inventory management, and planning for emergency demand spikes. Everything is written for a business owner operating with real cash-flow constraints, unreliable power, and informal supply chains.

1. Hiring and Training Local Women

In most African settings, women already manage household food processing, so they bring practical knowledge of sorting, drying, and hygiene. Hiring locally reduces transport costs, increases retention, and builds community trust. Start with a clear role description: sorter, roaster, miller, mixer, sealer, or packer. Pay a transparent daily or piece rate and comply with local labour rules. Train in two stages: first, a half-day orientation on food safety, handwashing, hair covering, and the difference between fortified and unfortified porridge; second, on-the-job certification where each worker must pass a simple visual check before working unsupervised. Cross-train at least two people per station so absence does not stop production.

Use a simple training record. It protects your business if a buyer audits you and it motivates workers who see a path to senior operator. Where literacy is limited, use pictures and demonstration rather than written manuals. Pair an experienced worker with a new hire for the first week and pay a small training bonus to the mentor.

2. Setting Up a Simple Production Line

A production line does not need stainless steel everywhere. It needs one-way flow: raw materials enter at one end, finished sealed bags leave at the other, with no crossing back. A typical layout is: receiving and weighing â cleaning and sorting â roasting or drying â milling â blending with vitamin-mineral premix â packaging and sealing â labelling and storage. Keep wet areas away from dry areas. Place the mixer and sealer close together to reduce handling. Use colour-coded buckets and scoops so the premix scoop is never used for maize.

Set a daily target in kilograms and track actual output on a chalkboard. If output falls below target for three days, investigate before blaming workers: check moisture content, grinder wear, and premix clumping. A simple line with five workers can often produce 200â400 kg per day once flow is smooth.

3. Buying or Renting Larger Equipment

Decide based on throughput, power, and maintenance. A diesel-powered hammer mill at 500 kg/hour costs far more than a 100 kg/hour electric mill, but it works during outages. Renting a mill for a day can be cheaper than owning if you produce fewer than eight days a month. For mixers, a horizontal ribbon blender gives more uniform premix distribution than a hand-mixed drum, which matters because vitamin A and iron must be evenly spread to avoid toxic over-doses in some portions.

For sealers, a continuous band sealer is faster and more consistent than an impulse sealer for 1 kg bags. Buy two of the cheapest critical machine rather than one expensive unit: if the sealer fails, production stops. Keep a spare grinder screen, belts, and heating element in stock. Before buying, ask for a demonstration with your own maize and soy, not the seller's sample.

Table 1. Equipment options for small and growing producers
EquipmentTypical capacityBuy vs rentKey maintenance
Hammer mill (electric)100â300 kg/hourBuy if milling 3+ days/weekReplace screens, check belts
Hammer mill (diesel)300â800 kg/hourBuy for off-grid or emergency supplyFuel, oil, air filter
Ribbon blender50â200 kg/batchBuy when premix is used dailyClean after each batch, check seals
Continuous band sealerUp to 1,000 bags/hourBuy two units if possibleHeating element, Teflon tape
Moisture meterHandheldBuy; low cost, high valueCalibrate monthly

Sources: FAO, Small-scale food processing technical notes; Practical Action, Appropriate Technology equipment briefs; manufacturer specifications.

4. Quality Control Checks at Each Step

Quality control is not a laboratory. It is a set of simple checks that stop bad product before it reaches a child. At receiving, check moisture (target below 12â13% for maize and soy) and smell for mould. At cleaning, remove stones, mouldy kernels, and foreign matter. At roasting, check that soy is properly heated to reduce trypsin inhibitors; under-roasted soy causes poor digestion. At milling, check particle size: too coarse and children cannot eat it; too fine and it dusts. At blending, verify premix weight with a scale and mix for the full time. At sealing, check seal strength by pulling a sample bag. At storage, keep bags off the floor on pallets, away from walls, and rotate stock first-in-first-out.

Aflatoxin is the biggest hidden risk in maize and groundnuts. Buy from suppliers who dry and store properly, reject discoloured or mouldy grain, and test with rapid kits where available. Never blend mouldy grain into a batch to save money; the reputational and health cost is far higher than the loss.

SAFETY WARNING â Vitamin and mineral premix is not ordinary flour.

Over-dosing iron, vitamin A, or zinc can seriously harm a child. Never use a scoop from another ingredient for premix. Weigh premix on a scale accurate to 0.1 g, record every batch, and store premix locked away from food and children. If you change premix supplier or concentration, recalculate the dose and test a small batch before full production. If a batch is suspected of over-dosing, stop sale immediately and seek advice from a nutritionist or public health officer.

5. Managing Inventory of Ingredients and Packaging

Inventory is cash sitting on a shelf. Too little and you stop production; too much and you tie up money and risk spoilage. Set a reorder point for each item: maize, soy, sugar or oil where used, premix, bags, labels, and cartons. The reorder point equals average daily use multiplied by lead time plus a safety stock. For imported premix with a two-month lead time, hold at least six weeks of stock. For local maize, hold two to four weeks depending on harvest season and price.

Use a simple stock card or a notebook: date in, quantity in, date out, quantity out, balance. Count physical stock weekly and compare with the card. Record losses and investigate. Keep packaging dry and away from sunlight because printed labels fade and bags weaken. Store premix in a cool, dark, locked place and respect expiry dates.

Table 2. Indicative reorder planning for a producer using 100 kg maize and 30 kg soy per day
ItemDaily useLead timeSafety stockReorder point
Maize100 kg7 days7 days1,400 kg
Soy30 kg10 days7 days510 kg
Premix2 kg45 days14 days118 kg
1 kg bags130 units14 days7 days2,730 units
Labels130 units10 days7 days2,210 units

Sources: Calculations based on standard inventory reorder-point formula; lead times are illustrative and should be replaced with your own supplier data. Premix handling guidance from UNICEF/WHO Fortification of complementary foods technical documents.

6. Planning for Increased Demand During Emergencies

Emergencies â floods, drought, displacement, disease outbreaks â create sudden demand from clinics, NGOs, and relief agencies. They also disrupt supply. Prepare before the crisis. Keep a standby list of trained workers who can work extra shifts. Hold a buffer of at least two weeks of finished product if you have dry storage. Pre-print labels with batch and date fields left blank. Agree in advance with a transporter and a backup transporter. Keep contact details for two premix suppliers and two maize suppliers.

When an emergency order arrives, confirm specification, quantity, delivery date, and payment terms in writing. Do not promise more than your line can produce at quality. It is better to deliver 2 tonnes on time than 5 tonnes late and unsafe. If demand exceeds capacity, consider a temporary second shift rather than rushing the line. Document every batch so you can trace it if a problem appears.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Train every worker on handwashing, hair covering, and premix safety before they touch production.
  • Keep one-way flow: raw materials in one end, sealed bags out the other, no crossing back.
  • Check moisture, mould, and foreign matter at receiving; reject suspect grain.
  • Weigh premix on a 0.1 g scale and record every batch.
  • Test seal strength and bag weight every hour during packaging.
  • Use stock cards, count weekly, and keep premix locked and cool.
  • Hold a two-week buffer of finished product and a standby worker list for emergencies.
  • Never blend mouldy grain or over-dose premix to save money.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Food safety and quality (official guidance and codes of practice).
  • WHO â Food safety (including complementary feeding and aflatoxin resources).
  • Codex Alimentarius â Codes of practice and standards (CAC/RCP 21-1979 for foods for infants and children).
  • UNICEF â Nutrition (complementary food fortification and emergency nutrition).
  • Practical Action â Appropriate technology and food processing (equipment and small enterprise guides).
